title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows a general-purpose AI coding and agent tool being used as an active component in adversarial intrusion operations. The Aurora ransomware group directed Cursor Agent, which runs on Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation steps against target organizations. The failure mode is not one of the AI system malfunctioning but of a legitimate deployed tool being used outside the conditions its developers intended, specifically as an instrument of unauthorized access rather than assisted software development.

The tool had no apparent control in place that prevented it from executing exploitation tasks when directed by malicious operators. A safeguard designed to detect or refuse instructions consistent with unauthorized computer access, such as commands to exploit vulnerabilities in live production systems, could have interrupted this use. Whether such safeguards existed and were bypassed, or were absent entirely, is not established by the reporting.

What is not established is whether Cursor or Anthropic had prior knowledge of this abuse, whether any platform-level detection flagged the activity during the period in question, and the full scope of victim harm attributable specifically to the AI-assisted steps as distinct from other techniques the group employed.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that the Aurora ransomware group, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi virtual machine environments. The group operates a data leak site and has victimized organizations across multiple countries. Researchers found that Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against ten target organizations between April and May 2026. The ESXi ransomware uses ChaCha20 encryption and includes an ESXi-specific mode that kills running virtual machines to access their disk files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can read ransom demands.

In a separate operation, researchers identified a second Aurora cluster with medium confidence, affecting eight victim organizations across Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This cluster used different techniques including SQL Server exploitation, privilege escalation with GodPotato, and data exfiltration to S3-compatible storage. Gambit Security provided technical indicators of compromise and details about Aurora's infrastructure, including command and control servers, proxy servers, and the group's onion site for victim negotiations.
